I am 71 years old this year, and I have never spent a single day in school. I cannot read a newspaper, but I can read this land with my hands and my feet. My father farmed these fields, and his father before him. For over fifty years I have watched the seasons turn in Quzhou, and I know what this soil wants. At my age, I do not have the strength or the heart to gamble on strange new crops—what if the market forgets to buy them? Wheat and corn are the only crops I trust. The grain station always takes them, and I can sell what my wife and I do not eat. I have four mu of land, and I will keep to the old rotation: winter wheat planted in the autumn, then summer corn seeded right after the wheat comes out in June. My neighbors mostly do the same, and when an old man farms alone, it is safer to follow the crowd. I buy my wheat seeds from the supply store—the improved varieties that have done well here for years—and for corn I use the hybrid seeds like Denghai or Nongda that everyone recommends. I rotary-till the wheat field before sowing, but for corn there is no time to waste after harvest, so I plant without plowing. I irrigate the wheat three or four times—sowing water, green-up water, and jointing water, plus maybe one more if the spring is dry—and the corn gets two good irrigations in the summer. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer the way I have always done: a bag and a half per mu for the wheat, with some ammonium bicarbonate thrown in, and a bit less for the corn. I spray for weeds and insects two or three times each season, when I see them coming. I am not chasing record yields anymore. If I get about 500 kilograms per mu of wheat and 600 kilograms per mu of corn, that is enough for an old man to live on and pay for medicine.
